title: Allocating Decoder Depth across Tokens
question: Under a hard budget on the mean fraction of decoder depth per token, pick the per-token signal and threshold that says a token can exit now.
elab:
Tokens differ in how much computation they need; the task develops an early-exit criterion that spends decoder depth on harder predictions while preserving language quality within a fixed average-depth budget.

A decoder trained so its intermediate layers can emit tokens does not have to run to the bottom for every token, but exiting early only buys depth if it exits on the right tokens, and in generation an early exit changes the states every later token is computed from. Under a hard budget on the mean fraction of decoder depth per generated token, the question is which per-token signal (softmax margin, hidden-state saturation, a fixed layer) should decide that a token is done, and how its threshold should be calibrated. It matters because adaptive depth is one of the few inference savings that does not require a smaller model.

description_md:
# The Exit Criterion for an Early-Exit Decoder

## Research Question

A decoder trained so that its intermediate layers can emit tokens does not have
to run to the bottom for every token: the shared final norm and unembedding can
be applied at any layer. Exiting early saves depth only if you exit on the right
tokens. Given a hard budget on the **mean fraction of the decoder executed per
generated token**, which per-token signal should decide that a token is done, and
how should the threshold on that signal be calibrated so that greedy generation
spends the budget and stays as close as possible to what the full-depth model
would have written?

## Background

CALM (Schuster, Fisch, Gupta, Dehghani, Bahri, Tran, Tay & Metzler, *Confident
Adaptive Language Modeling*, NeurIPS 2022, arXiv:2207.07061) proposes per-token
confidence measures for exactly this decision: the difference between the top
two softmax probabilities, the cosine saturation of the hidden state between
consecutive layers, and a small learned classifier. It argues that the threshold
should **decay with the decoding step** (its Eq. 5), because an early mistake
propagates through everything generated after it, and it **propagates the
exited token's hidden state** to the skipped layers so that later tokens can
still attend to it. It calibrates the threshold by running the adaptive model on
a calibration set. LayerSkip (Elhoushi et al., *LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit
Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding*, ACL 2024, arXiv:2404.16710) trains
models so that every layer can exit (layer dropout plus an early-exit loss on
the shared head); its released inference exits every token at one fixed layer.

Both papers evaluate early exit the same way: greedy **generation** with exits,
quality of the generated text (ROUGE), and cost as the average number of decoder
layers per generated token. The open question is which signal and which
calibration buy the most fidelity at a matched average depth, when an exit at one
token changes the states every later token is computed from.

## What You Can Modify

`layerskip-ee-lab/mlsee/exit_rule.py`, the editable region only (between the
`BEGIN EDITABLE REGION` / `END EDITABLE REGION` markers). It defines two
functions, run in one persistent, unprivileged process that is not given a GPU:

```python
def calibrate(cal, budget, n_layers, seed, simulate) -> dict
def should_exit(layer_idx, feat, state) -> np.ndarray   # (m,) bool
```

* `calibrate` gets every layer's features for every token of a full-depth
  greedy decoding of held-out **calibration** prompts, and a `simulate(state)`
  callable. Each `simulate` call runs the real early-exit decoder on the
  calibration prompts with `should_exit(., ., state)` and returns the realised
  `mean_depth`, `consistency_rougeL` (ROUGE-L against the full-depth
  calibration outputs), `rougeL_ref`, `n_tokens`, and per-token `exit_layer`,
  `seq`, `step`. It is expensive and limited to `cal["max_simulations"]`
  calls.
* `should_exit` is called at every decoding step and every layer, in decoding
  order, for the tokens of the scored prompts still running at that layer. It
  never sees a deeper layer of a token before deciding. Tokens still running
  after the second-to-last layer exit at the last one. `state` is the same dict
  object across calls, so a rule may keep online statistics.

Per (layer, token) you get: the post-norm `hidden` state and the previous
layer's `prev_hidden`, the pre-norm residual-stream state `resid` and the
previous layer's `prev_resid`, the 8 largest logits (`top_val`, `top_id`), the
`logsumexp` (so any softmax quantity of the top-8 is recoverable), the decoding
`step`, the prompt index `seq`, plus `n_layers`, `budget` and `max_new_tokens`.
You never see the reference outputs, the full-depth output of a scored prompt,
or a deeper layer of a running token.

An exited token's hidden state is propagated to the deeper layers (CALM's state
propagation), and the token is emitted from the shared head at its exit layer.
Generation is greedy and stops at a newline or end-of-sequence.

**The depth budget is measured, not declared.** The decoder records the layer
every generated token actually exited at, and BOTH of these must be within the
budget:

```
sum over generated tokens of (exit_layer + 1)
---------------------------------------------   <=  budget     (per generated token:
n_layers x (tokens you generated)                               CALM's cost metric)

sum over generated tokens of (exit_layer + 1)
---------------------------------------------   <=  budget     (per full-depth token)
n_layers x (tokens the full-depth model generated)
```

so neither padding an output with cheap tokens nor cutting it short buys depth.

A run over the budget scores nothing on that setting (the gate is strict: no
tolerance beyond floating-point rounding). The budget is passed to `calibrate` and is in `feat`; read it rather
than assuming it, because it differs between settings. Both functions must be
deterministic given `seed`.

**`exit_rule.py` itself must stay under 32768 bytes**, so that it holds an
algorithm rather than a table.

`numpy` and the standard library are available (torch imports, but the rule
process is not given a GPU). The vendored LayerSkip sources under
`/workspace/layerskip-ee-lab/` are readable reference, including the released
fixed-exit forward in `self_speculation/llama_model_utils.py`. There is no
network.

## Fixed Pipeline

Everything outside the two functions is fixed by the harness
(`mlsee/ee_decode.py`, `mlsee/rule_server.py`): which LayerSkip-trained
models are used, which prompts are generated from and scored, the features, the
decoding loop, the budget check and the scoring. The decoder runs in a separate
privileged process that alone holds the model, the prompts and the references.

## Evaluation

Three settings (`set_a`, `set_b` and `set_c`) that differ in the model,
the text and the depth budget. Reported per setting:

| metric | meaning | direction |
|---|---|---|
| `rougeL` | ROUGE-L F1 of the early-exit generations against the reference outputs | higher is better (scored) |
| `consistency_rougeL` | ROUGE-L F1 of the early-exit generations against the same model's full-depth generations (CALM's textual consistency) | higher is better (scored) |
| `rouge2` | ROUGE-2 F1 against the references | reported |
| `mean_depth` | the larger of the two depth normalisations above | gated by the budget |
| `exact_match_full` | fraction of prompts whose early-exit output equals the full-depth output | reported |

## Reference Baselines

* `calm_softmax` — CALM's softmax response (top-1 minus top-2 probability)
  with its position-adjusted threshold (tau = 4), ported from the released
  CALM code (google-research/t5x `t5x/contrib/calm`; arXiv:2207.07061).
* `calm_saturation` — CALM's hidden-state saturation: the cosine between
  consecutive layers' pre-norm decoder states, constant threshold (tau = 0),
  first exit at the second layer, from the same released code.
* `layerskip_fixed` — LayerSkip's released early-exit inference: every token
  exits at a fixed layer (two adjacent fixed layers mixed so that the arm
  spends the same budget as the others)
  (`self_speculation/llama_model_utils.py`, arXiv:2404.16710); also CALM's
  static baseline.
* `random_depth` — a null: the budget spent at random, reading nothing but the
  seed.
* `default` — the unmodified starter file: CALM's maximum-softmax-probability
  measure with a constant threshold (the released CALM code's default
  `conf_method='softmax_max'`).

Every reference arm uses the same budget calibration (bisection with all of
the simulations, aiming just under the budget); only the signal and the
threshold shape differ.

Wall-clock time is not scored: the budget is a counted depth, not a duration.

"""When should a decoder stop computing a token and emit what it already has?

The model is a decoder-only LM trained with LayerSkip's recipe (layer dropout
plus an early-exit loss on the shared head), so every layer's hidden state can
be turned into a next-token distribution with the shared final norm and LM
head.  Generation is greedy and token by token.  For every generated token the
decoder runs layer 0, 1, 2, ... and after each layer asks YOUR rule whether
this token is done.  If the rule says yes at layer l, the token is emitted
from layer l, and its layer-l hidden state is propagated to the deeper layers
(CALM's state propagation), so later tokens attend to keys/values computed
from that copied state.  An early mistake therefore changes everything that is
generated after it.

The evaluation runs your code in TWO STAGES, in one persistent CPU process:

  1. CALIBRATE  ``calibrate(cal, budget, n_layers, seed, simulate)`` gets
     every layer's features for every token of a full-depth greedy decoding
     of held-out CALIBRATION prompts, and a ``simulate(state)`` callable.
     Each ``simulate`` call runs the REAL early-exit decoder on the
     calibration prompts using ``should_exit(., ., state)`` and returns the
     realised mean depth and ROUGE-L consistency with the full-depth
     calibration outputs.  It is expensive and limited to
     ``cal["max_simulations"]`` calls.  Return the state for stage 2.
  2. EXIT       ``should_exit(layer_idx, feat, state)`` is called at every
     decoding step and every layer, in decoding order, for the tokens of
     the SCORED prompts that are still running at that layer.  It never
     sees a deeper layer of a token before deciding.  Tokens still running
     after the second-to-last layer exit at the last one.  ``state`` is the
     same dict object across calls, so a rule may keep online statistics.

The budget is on COMPUTE, measured by the decoder from the exit layers it
actually used, under two normalisations that must BOTH be within budget:

    sum over generated tokens of (exit_layer + 1)
    ---------------------------------------------   <=  budget
    n_layers x (tokens YOU generated)

    sum over generated tokens of (exit_layer + 1)
    ---------------------------------------------   <=  budget
    n_layers x (tokens the FULL-DEPTH model generated for the same prompts)

so neither padding an output nor cutting it short buys depth.

Over budget (the gate is strict) and the setting scores nothing.
Scored: ROUGE-L of the early-exit generations against the reference outputs,
and ROUGE-L against the same model's full-depth generations (consistency).
Neither the references nor the full-depth outputs of scored prompts are ever
shown to this process.  Both functions must be deterministic given ``seed``.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import sys

import numpy as np

# Available: numpy and the Python standard library (torch is importable but
# this process is not given a GPU).  There is no network.


# ==================================================================
# FIXED -- DO NOT MODIFY ABOVE THIS LINE
# ==================================================================

# ----- BEGIN EDITABLE REGION -----
# Replace everything between the BEGIN/END markers.  You may add helper
# functions, classes and imports (numpy / the standard library) inside this
# region.
#
# The starting implementation is CALM's maximum-softmax-probability measure
# (the released CALM code's default, t5x/contrib/calm/models.py conf_method=
# 'softmax_max', lines ~212-216): one constant threshold on the top-1
# probability at each layer.  Its budget calibration (below) is the one every
# reference arm uses: bisection with all of the real simulations.

# ---- budget calibration shared by every reference arm (identical code) ------
# Bisection on the arm's one scalar parameter with ALL of the task's real
# simulations, keeping the simulated operating point closest to (and not over)
# budget - _GAP.  Only the signal and the threshold shape differ between arms.
_GAP = 0.02           # aim this far under the budget: the gate is strict and the
                      # scored prompts drift from the calibration prompts


def _bisect(cal, budget, simulate, make, lo, hi, deeper_when_higher=True):
    target = budget - _GAP
    pts = []
    a, b = lo, hi
    for _ in range(int(cal["max_simulations"])):
        mid = 0.5 * (a + b)
        r = simulate(make(mid))
        pts.append((mid, float(r["mean_depth"])))
        if (r["mean_depth"] > target) == deeper_when_higher:
            b = mid
        else:
            a = mid
    feas = [p for p in pts if p[1] <= target]
    best = max(feas, key=lambda p: p[1]) if feas else min(pts, key=lambda p: p[1])
    return make(best[0])
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def _max_prob(top_val, logsumexp):
    """P(argmax) at this layer, from the top logits and the log-partition."""
    return np.exp(np.asarray(top_val[..., 0], dtype=np.float32)
                  - np.asarray(logsumexp, dtype=np.float32))


def calibrate(cal, budget, n_layers, seed, simulate):
    """Fit the exit threshold so the realised depth lands on ``budget``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    cal : dict over the calibration prompts' full-depth greedy decoding
        ``top_val``   (n_layers, n, k) float16, the k largest logits
        ``top_id``    (n_layers, n, k) int32, their vocabulary ids
        ``logsumexp`` (n_layers, n) float32
        ``step``      (n,) int32, the decoding step of each token
        ``seq``       (n,) int64, which calibration prompt it belongs to
        ``hidden``, ``resid`` (n_layers, s, d) float16: post-norm / pre-norm
                      states of the s tokens listed in ``state_index`` (a
                      fixed subsample of the n tokens)
        ``n_full_tokens``, ``max_new_tokens``, ``max_simulations`` (scalars)
    budget : float      the depth budget, in (0, 1]
    n_layers : int
    seed : int
    simulate : callable(state) -> dict
        Runs the real early-exit decoder on the calibration prompts with
        ``should_exit(., ., state)``.  Returns ``mean_depth`` (the gated
        quantity, max of ``depth_own`` and ``depth_full``), ``depth_own``,
        ``depth_full``, ``consistency_rougeL``, ``rougeL_ref``, ``n_tokens`` and
        per-token arrays ``exit_layer``, ``seq``, ``step``.

    Returns
    -------
    dict -- handed to every ``should_exit`` call (the same object each time).
    """
    return _bisect(cal, budget, simulate, lambda p: {"p": p}, 0.0, 1.0)


def should_exit(layer_idx, feat, state):
    """Decide, for every token still running, whether to stop at this layer.

    Parameters
    ----------
    layer_idx : int    0-based; the last layer is never asked (it is forced)
    feat : dict over the tokens still running at this layer
        ``hidden``      (m, d) float16, this layer's post-norm hidden state
        ``prev_hidden`` (m, d) float16, the previous layer's (zeros at layer 0)
        ``resid``       (m, d) float16, this layer's pre-norm residual state
        ``prev_resid``  (m, d) float16, the previous layer's (zeros at layer 0)
        ``top_val``     (m, k) float16, ``top_id`` (m, k) int32
        ``logsumexp``   (m,) float32
        ``step``        (m,) int32, the decoding step
        ``seq``         (m,) int64, which prompt the token belongs to
        ``n_layers``, ``budget``, ``max_new_tokens``
    state : dict       whatever ``calibrate`` returned

    Returns
    -------
    (m,) bool array -- True to emit this token from this layer.
    """
    return _max_prob(feat["top_val"], feat["logsumexp"]) >= state["p"]
# ----- END EDITABLE REGION -----

# ==================================================================
# FIXED -- DO NOT MODIFY BELOW THIS LINE
# ==================================================================

if __name__ == "__main__":  # pragma: no cover - the harness imports this module
    sys.stderr.write("exit_rule.py is imported by the harness, not run directly\n")
    sys.exit(2)

"""LayerSkip's released early-exit inference: every token exits at a fixed layer.

Paper: M. Elhoushi et al., "LayerSkip", ACL 2024, arXiv:2404.16710, Sec. 4.2 /
6.2.  Reference code: facebookresearch/LayerSkip@494752e5
self_speculation/llama_model_utils.py `forward_early` (lines 213-275): run
layers [0, exit_layer) and apply the shared norm + LM head -- the task's
harness reproduces this path exactly (fp32 check).  Also CALM's
"static" baseline (Sec. 5).
Budget matching: a single integer exit layer cannot spend a fractional budget,
so the arm uses a fractional exit layer x: each token exits at floor(x) or
floor(x)+1 (deterministic per-token hash, fraction frac(x) at the deeper one),
calibrated by the shared budget calibration so that it spends
the same depth as every other arm.  Verdict: DEVIATES (two adjacent fixed
layers mixed to match the budget; each token still uses LayerSkip's fixed-exit
forward).
"""
from pathlib import Path

_FILE = "layerskip-ee-lab/mlsee/exit_rule.py"
_SHARED = (Path(__file__).parent / "shared_calibration.py.txt").read_text()

_CONTENT = _SHARED + '''

def _uniform(seq, step):
    x = (np.asarray(seq, np.uint64) * np.uint64(0x9E3779B97F4A7C15)
         ^ np.asarray(step, np.uint64) * np.uint64(0xBF58476D1CE4E5B9))
    x ^= x >> np.uint64(31)
    x *= np.uint64(0x94D049BB133111EB)
    x ^= x >> np.uint64(29)
    return (x >> np.uint64(11)).astype(np.float64) / float(1 << 53)


def calibrate(cal, budget, n_layers, seed, simulate):
    return _bisect(cal, budget, simulate, lambda x: {"p": x}, 0.0, float(n_layers - 1))


def should_exit(layer_idx, feat, state):
    x = state["p"]
    base = int(np.floor(x))
    with np.errstate(over="ignore"):
        u = _uniform(feat["seq"], feat["step"])
    exit_layer = np.where(u < x - base, base + 1, base)
    fire = layer_idx >= exit_layer
    return fire
'''

"""When should a decoder stop computing a token and emit what it already has?

The model is a decoder-only LM trained with LayerSkip's recipe (layer dropout
plus an early-exit loss on the shared head), so every layer's hidden state can
be turned into a next-token distribution with the shared final norm and LM
head.  Generation is greedy and token by token.  For every generated token the
decoder runs layer 0, 1, 2, ... and after each layer asks YOUR rule whether
this token is done.  If the rule says yes at layer l, the token is emitted
from layer l, and its layer-l hidden state is propagated to the deeper layers
(CALM's state propagation), so later tokens attend to keys/values computed
from that copied state.  An early mistake therefore changes everything that is
generated after it.

The evaluation runs your code in TWO STAGES, in one persistent CPU process:

  1. CALIBRATE  ``calibrate(cal, budget, n_layers, seed, simulate)`` gets
     every layer's features for every token of a full-depth greedy decoding
     of held-out CALIBRATION prompts, and a ``simulate(state)`` callable.
     Each ``simulate`` call runs the REAL early-exit decoder on the
     calibration prompts using ``should_exit(., ., state)`` and returns the
     realised mean depth and ROUGE-L consistency with the full-depth
     calibration outputs.  It is expensive and limited to
     ``cal["max_simulations"]`` calls.  Return the state for stage 2.
  2. EXIT       ``should_exit(layer_idx, feat, state)`` is called at every
     decoding step and every layer, in decoding order, for the tokens of
     the SCORED prompts that are still running at that layer.  It never
     sees a deeper layer of a token before deciding.  Tokens still running
     after the second-to-last layer exit at the last one.  ``state`` is the
     same dict object across calls, so a rule may keep online statistics.

The budget is on COMPUTE, measured by the decoder from the exit layers it
actually used, under two normalisations that must BOTH be within budget:

    sum over generated tokens of (exit_layer + 1)
    ---------------------------------------------   <=  budget
    n_layers x (tokens YOU generated)

    sum over generated tokens of (exit_layer + 1)
    ---------------------------------------------   <=  budget
    n_layers x (tokens the FULL-DEPTH model generated for the same prompts)

so neither padding an output nor cutting it short buys depth.

Over budget (the gate is strict) and the setting scores nothing.
Scored: ROUGE-L of the early-exit generations against the reference outputs,
and ROUGE-L against the same model's full-depth generations (consistency).
Neither the references nor the full-depth outputs of scored prompts are ever
shown to this process.  Both functions must be deterministic given ``seed``.

import sys

import numpy as np
